qs.q: A 50-year-old male presents with a history of chronic diarrhoea, weight loss, and abdominal pain. Small bowel biopsy shows villous atrophy, increased intraepithelial lymphocytes, and positive anti-tTG antibodies. What is the most appropriate long-term management?
qs.e: The diagnosis of celiac disease, confirmed by biopsy and serology, requires a lifelong gluten-free diet to manage symptoms and prevent complications.

faq.a: It signals mucosal inflammation, often due to infection, malnutrition, or autoimmune disease like celiac.
faq.q: What does an increased IEL count indicate?

faq.a: A small number of IELs is normal; counts >25 per 100 cells are abnormal.
faq.q: Can IELs be increased in normal individuals?

faq.a: No; microscopic disease can be present despite a normal mucosal appearance, so biopsy is required.
faq.q: Is a normal endoscopy enough to rule out disease?

exam: What is the first investigation you would order in a patient with chronic diarrhoea and suspected IEL increase? — Stool microscopy for parasites and HIV rapid test to identify common tropical causes.
How would you differentiate lymphocytic colitis from collagenous colitis on biopsy? — Look for a dense subepithelial collagen layer in collagenous; lymphocytic shows >1 IEL per 5 colonocytes.
Why is a gluten‑free diet recommended in celiac disease? — It removes the antigen that drives IEL proliferation and villous atrophy.
What red flag would prompt urgent referral from a ward round? — Rapid weight loss with severe anaemia indicating malabsorption.
Which drug class should be avoided in a patient with severe diarrhoea and suspected mucosal inflammation? — Anticholinergic agents, as they worsen constipation and mucosal perfusion.

How would you manage a patient with IEL increase but no access to endoscopy? — Treat empirically for common infections (antiparasitics, antibiotics) and provide nutritional support while arranging referral.
ai.title: Intraepithelial Lymphocytes
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Intraepithelial lymphocytes (IELs) are immune cells residing in the gut epithelium. Their abnormal increase signals mucosal inflammation, seen in celiac disease, microscopic colitis, and infections common in low‑resource settings.

b: IELs are identified on biopsy by their location and morphology.
sections.p: IELs are T‑cell lymphocytes located between epithelial cells of the intestinal mucosa. Histology shows them as round cells in the epithelial layer.
Severity is graded by the number of IELs per 100 epithelial cells. A count >25 per 100 cells is abnormal; >50 indicates severe inflammation.

t.b: Counts IELs per 100 epithelial cells – >25 indicates pathology

sections.p: In low‑resource settings, infections (tuberculosis, schistosomiasis, HIV), malnutrition, and parasitic infestations are common triggers. Autoimmune conditions like celiac disease are less frequent but still present.
Patients may have chronic diarrhoea, abdominal pain, weight loss, or be asymptomatic with incidental findings on endoscopy.
Endoscopy with duodenal or colonic biopsies is essential. In resource‑limited settings, a simple stool exam and HIV test can guide management when biopsy is unavailable.
Severe malabsorption can lead to anaemia, osteoporosis, and growth failure. Untreated infections may progress to systemic disease.
Treat underlying cause: gluten withdrawal for celiac, antiparasitics for schistosomiasis, antiretrovirals for HIV. Supportive care includes nutrition and symptom control.
Repeat endoscopy in 6–12 months to assess mucosal healing. Preventive measures include sanitation, safe water, and vaccination where applicable.
Other causes of villous atrophy such as tropical sprue, Crohn’s disease, and infections can mimic IEL increase.

b: Low haemoglobin may not reflect malnutrition
Stool microscopy may be falsely negative
sections.p: In severe anaemia, haemoglobin may be low despite adequate nutrition. Stool microscopy can miss low‑level parasitic infections.
